stats.sign_convention: Positive values mean the ground moved toward the satellite (for example uplift); negative values mean it moved away from the satellite (for example subsidence).

detection.rule: range (1st to 99th percentile) > 9 x noise level for every processing choice, and again after planar ramp removal (or a ramp-removed spread above 5 cm); noise level kept between 1 and 2.5 cm

uncertainty.method: NASA GUNW unwrapped phase (HH, 80 m) converted to line-of-sight displacement with the 24.2 cm wavelength read from the file, NASA's ionosphere phase screen subtracted, masked where coherence is below 0.3, over water or not reliably unwrapped, referenced to the window median. Noise level from the robust spread (1.4826 x MAD); ranges from repeating the analysis with coherence thresholds 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.4, with and without the ionosphere correction, and with and without a planar ramp.
notes: Displacement is measured along the radar line of sight and is relative: the median of the usable pixels in the window (+14.5 cm before referencing) was set to zero. Positive values mean the ground moved toward the satellite (for example uplift); negative values mean it moved away from the satellite (for example subsidence).
Empirical noise level: the robust spread of the motion field (1.4826 x median absolute deviation) is 21.44 cm, and 14.03 to 24.73 cm across the processing choices.
A single 12-day pair typically carries about 1 to 2 cm of atmospheric noise, so smaller signals cannot be trusted. The noise level is therefore never taken below 1 cm.

Decision rule: motion is reported only if the 1st-to-99th percentile range exceeds 9 x the noise level (22.5 cm here) for every processing choice and the field still stands out after a planar ramp is removed (same test, or a spread above 5 cm). Ideal noise gives 4.65 x; 44 real NISAR pairs without an earthquake gave 2.6 to 6.9 x. Smallest range found: 57.3 cm; after ramp removal: 47.9 cm.
69% of the window was masked: 21% coherence below 0.3, 36% water, 12% not reliably unwrapped, 0% no data.

The field's spread (21.4 cm) is far larger than atmosphere can explain, so it is attributed to motion and the noise level is set to 2.5 cm, the largest value this workflow accepts as atmosphere, rather than measured. Scatter over short distances (2.6 km tiles) is 1.08 cm.

Ionosphere: NASA's ionosphere phase screen spans 13.2 cm across the usable area. NASA ships it as a separate layer and does not apply it; here it WAS subtracted. Without it the robust spread would be 15.85 cm instead of 21.44 cm. NASA's own uncertainty for that estimate is 3.7 cm (median).
Planar ramp: a best-fit plane changes by +30.1 cm from west to east and -35.9 cm from south to north across the window. It was kept (a ramp can be real motion).
Noise from loss of coherence alone is about 0.20 cm per pixel (median coherence 0.43, 208 looks): the noise here is mostly atmospheric, not instrumental.

caveats.text: This is motion along the radar's slanted line of sight, not vertical motion and not full 3-D motion. Horizontal and vertical movement are mixed together. The radar looked down at 43 degrees from vertical with the satellite to the west-north-west: one centimetre here is 0.73 x upward + -0.66 x eastward + +0.17 x northward motion.
Values are relative to the median of the usable pixels in the drawn area, not to a stable reference point. If the whole area moved together, that shared motion is invisible here.

Water vapour in the atmosphere delays the radar signal differently on the two dates and typically adds 1 to 2 cm of smooth, false motion to a single pair. No atmospheric (troposphere) correction was applied.
NISAR's L-band radar is strongly affected by the ionosphere. NASA's ionosphere estimate was subtracted, but that estimate has its own error and is interpolated across gaps.

Turning fringes into continuous motion (phase unwrapping) can slip by whole fringes of 12.1 cm across gaps of low coherence such as water, forest, steep slopes or a fault rupture. Sharp steps of about that size should be treated as suspect.
This pair is provisional-tier: calibrated, but values may change after NASA reprocesses it.

The pair spans only 12 days (17 June 2026 to 29 June 2026). It shows what moved between those two passes and cannot show slow motion, timing within the interval, or whether motion continued afterwards.

params.reference: median of the usable pixels in the window

receipt.reproduce:
# pip install -e backend/   (needs an Earthdata Login in ~/.netrc)
import numpy as np
from nisar_investigator import catalog, gunw

bbox = (-68.45, 10.3, -67.95, 10.75)  # west, south, east, north
granule_id = "NISAR_L2_PR_GUNW_023_054_D_083_024_4000_SH_20260617T230235_20260617T230310_20260629T230235_20260629T230309_P05023_N_F_J_001"
pair = next(g for g in catalog.search("GUNW", bbox=bbox) if g.granule_id == granule_id)
cut = gunw.read_window(pair, bbox)  # reads only this window over HTTPS

phase = cut.layers["unwrappedPhase"] - cut.layers["ionospherePhaseScreen"]  # NASA's ionosphere estimate, subtracted
los_cm = -cut.wavelength_m / (4 * np.pi) * phase * 100  # positive = toward the satellite
cc, mask = cut.layers["connectedComponents"], cut.layers["mask"]
ok = (np.isfinite(los_cm) & (cut.layers["coherenceMagnitude"] >= 0.3)
      & (cc != 0) & (cc != gunw.CC_FILL) & gunw.valid_sample_mask(mask) & ~gunw.water_mask(mask))
los_cm = np.where(ok, los_cm - np.median(los_cm[ok]), np.nan)  # relative to the window median

p1, p5, p95, p99 = np.nanpercentile(los_cm, [1, 5, 95, 99])
spread = 1.4826 * np.nanmedian(np.abs(los_cm - np.nanmedian(los_cm)))
print(f"robust spread {spread:.2f} cm, 5th-95th percentile span {p95 - p5:.2f} cm, "
      f"1st-99th percentile range {p99 - p1:.2f} cm, usable pixels {ok.mean():.1%}")

# or the whole workflow, with sensitivity analysis, maps and receipt:
from nisar_investigator.schemas import MotionRequest
from nisar_investigator.workflows.motion import run_motion
result = run_motion(MotionRequest(bbox=bbox, reference_date="2026-06-17", track=54))
print(result.summary.headline)

report.answer: The ground moved up to 48 to 66 cm along the radar line of sight between 17 and 29 June 2026, with 422.0 to 845.2 km² showing movement exceeding 2x the noise level (5.0 cm). This coincides with two major earthquakes (7.5 and 7.2 magnitude) on 24 June 2026, located within 150 km of the area.

possible_explanations: The ground movement was caused by the 24 June 2026 earthquakes. To check: Compare with seismic fault lines and check for post-earthquake aftershocks in the area.
The displacement reflects tectonic adjustments rather than direct earthquake effects. To check: Analyze long-term InSAR time series for pre- and post-earthquake trends.
unknown: Vertical displacement magnitude (line-of-sight data cannot separate vertical from horizontal components)
report.confidence: medium: Strong correlation between detected motion and nearby earthquakes, but line-of-sight limitation and potential atmospheric noise (up to 2.5 cm) reduce certainty.
